note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 35-year-old lawyer with new-onset, work-predominant frontal headaches plus intermittent palpitations, shortness of breath at rest, bilateral hand tingling, reduced appetite, mild unintentional weight loss (~5 lb), and decreased libido since changing jobs; plan is in-person exam and thyroid blood tests. DDx includes work-related anxiety/hyperventilation, thyroid dysfunction, and tension-type headache (consistent with transcript).

History:
- Presenting complaint: Severe headaches; additional intermittent symptoms include palpitations, shortness of breath while seated at desk, tingling in both hands/arms, reduced appetite, decreased libido, and mild unintentional weight loss (~5 lb).
- Timeline: Symptoms began around the time of a job change; ongoing.
- Pattern: Occur mainly during work (meetings, laptop use); elevator entry in the morning can trigger palpitations. Symptoms occur at different times rather than all together.
- Headache features:
  - Location: Mostly frontal; does not radiate.
  - Associated symptoms: Sometimes mild nausea.
  - Triggers/context: Often during work (meetings or laptop use); not noted on commute.
  - Prior history: No similar headaches before this period.
- Dyspnea:
  - Occurs while seated at desk; not with exercise.
- Palpitations:
  - Roughly once daily or more; noted with elevator in the morning.
- Paresthesias:
  - Tingling in both hands; not in legs; described as “quick picking.”
- Appetite/weight/libido:
  - Reduced appetite; ~5 lb unintentional weight loss; clothing not noticeably looser; no external comments on weight loss.
  - Decreased libido since job change.
- Stress: Rates current work stress 7–8/10; law firm setting with ongoing pressure.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No exertional shortness of breath.
  - No smoking or recreational drug use.
  - “Feeling hot” was listed in the booking note, but patient emphasized shortness of breath instead; heat intolerance not clearly endorsed.

Past Medical History:
- Patient-reported “hyperthyroidism”; taking thyroxine.
  - Conflict noted: Thyroxine (levothyroxine) is typically used for hypothyroidism; patient’s stated diagnosis vs medication suggests possible mislabeling of thyroid condition. Clarification needed.

Medications:
- Thyroxine (levothyroxine) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Medication adherence: Patient reports taking as prescribed.
- Allergies: Not recorded.

Social History:
- Occupation: Lawyer in London; mix of meetings and computer/reading work (~50/50).
- Alcohol: A couple of glasses of wine once weekly.
- Tobacco: Denies smoking.
- Recreational drugs: Denies use.
- Psychosocial: High occupational stress since job change.

Family History:
- Not recorded.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded (tele-visit; in-person exam planned).

Investigations:
- Planned: Blood tests for thyroid function (“for your thyroxine”).
- Results: None available.
- No other tests or imaging mentioned.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - New-onset, work-associated frontal headaches with intermittent palpitations, dyspnea at rest, bilateral hand tingling, diminished appetite, mild weight loss, and decreased libido since job change. Features and timing are consistent with work-related anxiety/hyperventilation and tension-type headaches; thyroid dysfunction remains a key alternative given thyroxine use and systemic symptoms.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Work-related anxiety/panic with hyperventilation: Onset after job change; symptoms cluster at work/elevator; dyspnea at rest and bilateral hand tingling support; no exertional symptoms.
  - Thyroid dysfunction (possible over-replacement): On thyroxine with weight loss, palpitations, decreased libido; however, symptoms are situational and heat intolerance not clearly endorsed.
  - Tension-type headache (stress/ergonomic): Frontal headaches during meetings/screen time; high stress; limited migrainous features.

- Issue 1: Recurrent frontal headaches affecting work (likely stress/ergonomic or anxiety-related; DDx as above)
  - Plan:
    - In-person appointment for evaluation.
    - No new medications prior to examination.

- Issue 2: Palpitations and shortness of breath at rest (situational; occurs at desk and in elevator; no exercise-induced symptoms)
  - Plan:
    - In-person cardiovascular and respiratory examination (as discussed).
    - No new medications prior to examination.

- Issue 3: Thyroid disease on thyroxine with systemic symptoms (weight loss, palpitations, decreased libido); diagnosis label vs medication suggests potential mismatch
  - Plan:
    - Order thyroid blood tests (thyroid function tests) to assess current thyroid status and appropriateness of thyroxine dosing.
    - Review medication indication once lab results available.

- General plan items:
  - Patient to book an in-person clinic appointment via the app.
  - Clinician will inform colleagues of today’s history to avoid repetition.
  - Defer any new treatments until after in-person assessment and labs.

Quality checks:
- Missing/expected elements:
  - Allergies not recorded.
  - Medication dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Vitals and physical examination not performed (tele-visit).
  - Family history and broader review of systems not recorded.
- Conflicts:
  - Patient reports “hyperthyroidism” but is taking thyroxine (typically for hypothyroidism) — conflict noted; requires clarification.
  - “Feeling hot” listed in appointment reason; patient emphasized shortness of breath instead; heat intolerance not clearly endorsed.
- Transcript quality:
  - Minor hesitations and incomplete phrases; overall history understandable and coherent.
